title: The gentle way off the phone: a seven-day plan to reduce screen time
description: How to reduce screen time gently: a seven-day plan for 3 to 7 year olds, and the screen-free times the Indian Academy of Pediatrics names.
author: Kheelona
heroAlt: A curly-haired girl in denim dungarees sits on a wooden floor by a sunlit window lined with potted plants, Kheelu in her lap, touching its chin with one finger.

sources.label: Indian Academy of Pediatrics, “Guidelines on Screen Time and Digital Wellness in Infants, Children and Adolescents”, Indian Pediatrics, 2022, p. 239.
American Academy of Pediatrics, Council on Communications and Media, “Media and Young Minds”, Pediatrics, 2016, Recommendations: Families.

content.text: Here it is as a seven-day plan. Start on any day of the week.
Why replace before you remove?
Nobody plans for their 4-year-old to find the video app faster than they can. It happens one busy evening at a time.
The phone came in because it solved something: a work call, a bored child, the queue at the clinic. Take it away without replacing what it did, and the gap turns into a fight.
So this plan replaces first and removes second.
What are you aiming for?

The Indian Academy of Pediatrics says at most one hour of supervised screen time a day from two to five. From five to ten, it says less than two hours a day, including screens used for homework. For both ages, it adds: “the lesser, the better”.[^1]
For children aged two to five, it also says not to use screens during meals, within an hour before sleep, or “during surface travel”: in the car, on the bus, on the train.[^1]
The American Academy of Pediatrics asks families of young children to keep bedrooms, mealtimes and playtime together screen-free, for parents as well as children.[^2]
You don’t need to get there this week. The plan starts with one slot. For the numbers age by age, read
How much screen time is okay for a young child?
Days 1 and 2: notice when the phone comes out
Change nothing yet. Notice when the phone appears: the morning rush, the cooking hour, the car, the queue at the clinic.
Each one is a job the phone was hired to do. Write them down. That list is your plan for the week.
Days 3 and 4: replace the easiest slot

Pick the slot where the stakes are lowest. Fill it with something that talks back or keeps hands busy. A story, told or played aloud, in your home language. A grandparent on a voice call. A puzzle you started together at breakfast, waiting on the table.
Leave the hard slots alone for now. One calm win is worth more than three fights.
Need more ideas for the slot? Try
Busy hands, no screens
Days 5 and 6: shrink the rest, don’t snatch
In the slots that are left, end the screen at a natural break: the end of an episode, not the middle of a scene.
Then land it somewhere: a job, a snack, a spot-the-crow contest at the window. Have the next thing ready before the screen goes dark.
Try this:
before the screen goes on, say where it will land: “One episode, then we water the plants.”
If switching off is the hard part, read
Screen time and tantrums
Day 7: say the new rules out loud
Tell your child what changed, in the language you speak at home: mornings are for songs now, the car is for spotting autos, dinner is for talking.

Say it the same way every time, so it sounds like a rule, not a mood. And keep the rule yourself: at meals and at playtime together, the American Academy of Pediatrics suggests parents set their phones to “do not disturb”.[^2]
Week 2: expect a wobble
Some days will slip: a long journey, a sick day, a deadline. It happens. Go back to your list and pick up where you stopped.
Look at what your slots needed in the end: something to do, and someone to talk to, whether that is you, a grandparent or a sibling.
For the slots where your hands are full,
Kheelu

is one screen-free option. It is a plush toy for ages 3 to 7 that answers your child, then asks a question back, and you can read every conversation in the parent app. It is not a toy for children under 3. If your child is 3, keep a grown-up nearby while they play.

cardTitle: The gentle way off the phone: a seven-day plan
lead: A week-long plan to cut a young child’s screen time without turning your home into a battlefield.

answer.question: How do I reduce my child’s screen time?
answer.text: Go slowly, and fill the gap before you take anything away. Find the times of day the phone usually comes out, replace them one at a time with play, stories, songs or a small job, and stop screens at a natural break, not mid-episode. Keep meals and the hour before bed screen-free, for the grown-ups too.
